clinicalPearls: Consider Castleman disease when lymphadenopathy (localized or generalized) is accompanied by unexplained constitutional symptoms, cytopenias, or hypergammaglobulinemia.
Unicentric disease is usually indolent, presenting as a single enlarged lymph node mass, and is often curable with excision.
Multicentric disease is a systemic illness with fevers, weight loss, organomegaly, and multi-organ dysfunction driven by excess IL-6 signaling.
HHV-8 infection drives most multicentric cases in HIV-positive patients; idiopathic multicentric disease occurs without HHV-8 or HIV.
POEMS syndrome and TAFRO syndrome are important clinical variants/associations that change management and prognosis.
Excisional lymph node biopsy with expert hematopathology review is essential — needle biopsies are often non-diagnostic.
Multicentric disease carries an increased risk of progression to lymphoma and of concurrent Kaposi sarcoma in HHV-8-positive/HIV-positive patients.
harrison.pathophysiology: Castleman disease is a heterogeneous group of lymphoproliferative disorders characterized by distinctive lymph node architectural changes, most driven by dysregulated interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling. In unicentric disease the process is localized and follicular/vascular changes predominate, while multicentric disease reflects a systemic cytokine-driven process, frequently linked to lytic HHV-8 infection in immunocompromised hosts, producing viral IL-6 and human IL-6 that fuel plasmablast proliferation and systemic inflammation. Idiopathic multicentric disease lacks HHV-8 but shares a similar IL-6-driven inflammatory phenotype, sometimes with an associated clonal or autoimmune-like process.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune/rheumatologic disease with lymphadenopathy (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis)
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph node biopsy — required for definitive histopathologic diagnosis and subtype classification
HIV serology and HHV-8 testing (blood PCR or tissue staining) — identifies virus-associated multicentric disease
Complete blood count — screens for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or thrombocytosis seen in multicentric/TAFRO variants
Serum IL-6 and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) — supports the systemic inflammatory phenotype
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulin levels — assesses hypergammaglobulinemia and screens for paraproteins/POEMS
Cross-sectional imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) — defines extent of nodal disease and organomegaly, distinguishes unicentric from multicentric involvement
Renal and liver function testing — evaluates end-organ involvement from systemic cytokine excess
Bone marrow examination — helps exclude lymphoma or plasma cell dyscrasia when systemic disease is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive multi-organ failure (renal, hepatic) suggesting TAFRO syndrome
Concurrent Kaposi sarcoma or hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like picture
New neurologic findings or organomegaly suggesting POEMS syndrome
Rapid nodal growth or B symptoms raising concern for transformation to lymphoma
pitfalls: Attributing lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms solely to infection or malignancy without considering Castleman disease, delaying diagnosis
Relying on core needle biopsy alone, which frequently yields non-diagnostic or misleading architecture compared to excisional biopsy
Failing to test for HIV and HHV-8 in patients with multicentric disease, missing a treatable driver
Overlooking associated syndromes (POEMS, TAFRO) that substantially alter prognosis and treatment approach
harrison.prognosis: Unicentric Castleman disease has an excellent prognosis after complete surgical excision, with cure in most cases. Multicentric disease, particularly HHV-8-associated or TAFRO-variant forms, follows a more relapsing and potentially life-threatening course, with outcomes improved by IL-6-pathway-targeted therapy but still carrying elevated risk of lymphoma and organ dysfunction.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Peripheral Lymphadenopathy and Splenomegaly / Castleman Disease
management: Complete surgical excision for unicentric disease, which is usually curative.
Interleukin-6 pathway blockade with siltuximab, or tocilizumab, as first-line therapy for idiopathic multicentric disease.
Rituximab-based therapy, with antiretroviral therapy and consideration of antiviral treatment, for HHV-8-associated multicentric disease in HIV-positive patients.
Corticosteroids and, for aggressive or organ-threatening disease, cytotoxic chemotherapy.
Monitoring of inflammatory markers, blood counts and organ function, with attention to TAFRO and POEMS features.
Multidisciplinary haematology care with expert histopathology review, and escalation for cytokine-driven multi-organ failure.
